clinial_notes:
Clinical History

Alan is a 45-year-old male, an avid fitness enthusiast who started a new high-intensity interval training (HIIT) program two weeks ago. He increased his workout intensity significantly, aiming to overcome a weight plateau. Four days ago, after an intense session comprising repetitive high-load squats and sprints, Alan began experiencing severe muscle soreness beyond his usual discomfort. Notably, his urine turned dark, akin to cola color. He reports persistent pain chiefly in his thighs and calves, accompanied by swelling. Alan also reported weakness and difficulty walking.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - thigh muscles NPRS: 8-9

P2 - calves NPRS: 7

aggrevating factors: Walking, rising from a seated position, and any physical exertion.

easing factors: Laying supine with legs elevated, icing affected areas, and rest

past history Attempted a similar high-intensity workout regimen 2 years ago but experienced 'general soreness', no notable rhabdomyolysis symptoms were present.

medical history: No significant past medical history. No chronic diseases or previous surgeries. Reports taking protein supplements regularly.

medications: Occasional ibuprofen for muscle soreness

personal history: Alan works as an IT specialist and has a sedentary lifestyle outside his routine workouts. He lives with his partner and has a balanced diet, high in protein to support muscle building.

imaging: Recent ultrasounds have not been performed. Blood tests reveal elevated creatine kinase levels and myoglobinuria consistent with rhabdomyolysis.

clinial_notes:
Clinical History

John Carter is a 78-year-old retired factory worker who presented to the emergency department following a slip and fall on his kitchen floor. He immediately experienced severe left hip pain and was unable to bear weight. Emergency medical services found him lying supine, with the left leg shortened and externally rotated. He reports a history of occasional dizziness, most recently a week prior to the fall. On examination, the affected hip is tender to palpation, with marked restrictions in active and passive movement and significant guarding due to pain. Radiographs confirm a displaced intertrochanteric fracture of the left femur. He is scheduled for surgical fixation.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - Primary - Left hip region (deep, lateral, and groin) NPRS: 8-10

P2 - Secondary - Left thigh (proximal musculature), radiating pain NPRS: 4-5

aggrevating factors: Attempting to move or rotate the left lower limb, weight bearing, transferring between bed and chair, coughing or sneezing. Pain worsens with any movement of the hip.

easing factors: Application of cold packs, immobilization of the limb, administration of opioid analgesics, and remaining supine with minimal movement.

past history History of hypertension for 15 years, managed with medications. No previous falls recorded. Osteopenia noted in recent DEXA scan, but no prior fractures.

medical history: Hypertension (well-controlled), osteopenia, benign prostatic hyperplasia. No known cardiac or pulmonary comorbidities.

medications: Lisinopril 10mg daily, Hydrochlorothiazide 25mg daily, Tamsulosin 0.4mg at night, Acetaminophen as needed for headaches, Oxycodone 5mg every 4 hours PRN for hip pain since hospitalization.

personal history: Lives alone in a one-story home. Widowed 10 years ago. Three adult children, all living out of state. He manages independent self-care but requires a cane for outdoor ambulation. No tobacco or alcohol use.

imaging: AP and lateral radiographs of the pelvis and left hip confirm a displaced intertrochanteric fracture of the left femur. No head injury on CT. Pre-operative labs within normal limits.
title: Case Study: Mr. John Carter's Displaced Intertrochanteric Hip Fracture

clinial_notes:
Clinical History

Mrs. Jeanette K. is a 67-year-old retired librarian who presents with a gradual onset of right knee pain over the past 6 years, progressively worsening in the last 12 months. She reports stiffness in the morning lasting about 20 minutes, which eases with gentle movement. The pain is aggravated by walking long distances (more than one block), descending stairs, and rising from a low chair. She also experiences increased discomfort after periods of gardening or shopping. She notices crepitus with knee movement and mild swelling after heavy use, with no locking but occasional feelings of instability. She denies nocturnal pain unless she had an active day. There is no history of trauma, but she reports a history of being overweight (BMI 32) and a previous diagnosis of prediabetes.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - right medial tibiofemoral compartment (knee joint) NPRS: 5-7

P2 - right quadriceps (secondary muscle fatigue and aching after activity) NPRS: 2-3

aggrevating factors: Prolonged walking (>10 minutes), standing >15 minutes, descending stairs, rising from a low surface, cold/damp weather, gardening, shopping trips

easing factors: Short rest periods, gentle range of motion exercises, heat pack to knee, low-dose paracetamol, elevation after activity, swimming/aquatic exercise

past history Gradual increase in body weight over the last 20 years; mild, quickly resolving right knee sprain 8 years ago (no persistent injury), no prior joint surgeries or significant trauma.

medical history: Prediabetes diagnosed 5 years ago; hypertension well-controlled with medication; mild hypercholesterolemia.

medications: Paracetamol 500 mg as required (1-2/day), Lisinopril 10mg daily, Simvastatin 20mg nightly

personal history: Married, lives with spouse in a single-story home. Retired for 2 years, previously sedentary occupation. Hobbies include gardening, knitting, and volunteering at the local library. Limited formal exercise; recently started aquatic classes at the community pool.

imaging: Recent bilateral knee radiograph reveals medial joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation on the right knee consistent with moderate osteoarthritis. No evidence of acute fracture or inflammatory arthropathy.
title: Case Study: Mrs. Jeanette K. and Progressive Knee Osteoarthritis

His pain level exacerbates with certain movements like standing for more than 10-15 minutes or during prolonged walks. Occasionally, Mr. Johnson feels a grinding sensation in his hip joint. NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

Primary Pain - Right hip (groin and anterior thigh) NPRS: 6-8

aggrevating factors: Standing for more than 15 minutes, walking more than a few blocks, certain twisting motions, and rising after prolonged sitting.

easing factors: Mild movements, heat packs, and over-the-counter pain relief medication.

medical history: Mr. Johnson has managed high blood pressure for the past 7 years, which is well-controlled with medication.

medications: Acetaminophen as needed for pain relief. Lisinopril for hypertension.

personal history: Mr. Johnson lives with his wife of 42 years. He enjoys woodworking as a hobby, though his hip pain has limited his shop time recently. They have two adult children and three grandchildren who live nearby.

clinial_notes:
Clinical History

Michael is a 20-year-old male collegiate track and field athlete specializing in middle-distance running. He presents with a six-week history of insidious onset right anterior knee pain. The pain began after he increased his training volume and intensity, specifically adding hill repeats, in preparation for the upcoming indoor season. Initially, the pain was a mild, dull ache that he felt only after long runs, but it has progressively worsened. He now describes the pain (P1) as a constant ache 'behind the kneecap' that becomes sharp and grinding with specific movements. He reports a sensation of stiffness after periods of prolonged sitting, such as during his university lectures, and notes difficulty with stairs in his dormitory, particularly when descending. There is no history of a specific traumatic event, overt swelling, or sensations of the knee giving way. His sleep is generally undisturbed unless he sleeps with his knee significantly bent.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - Diffuse anterior knee, retropatellar (behind the kneecap). The primary affected structures are the patellofemoral joint and associated articular cartilage. Muscular contributors include the Quadriceps femoris group (vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, rectus femoris), with potential imbalances or tracking issues. NPRS: 2-3/10 at rest, 6-7/10 during aggravating activities.

aggrevating factors: Running (especially downhill or on canted surfaces), descending stairs, deep squatting, prolonged sitting with the knee flexed ('movie-goer's sign'), and resisted knee extension exercises.

easing factors: Complete rest, ice application following activity, straightening the leg after prolonged sitting, and occasional use of over-the-counter anti-inflammatories.

past history History of a Grade I left ankle sprain approximately one year ago. This resolved with self-management but may have contributed to subtle, chronic compensatory changes in his running mechanics. No prior history of significant knee injury or surgery.

medical history: Unremarkable. He is otherwise fit and healthy with no known chronic illnesses.

medications: Ibuprofen (Advil) 200-400mg taken as needed (prn) for pain, typically 3-4 times per week following training sessions.

personal history: Michael is a full-time university student on an athletic scholarship, which places considerable pressure on him to perform and remain healthy. He lives in a campus dormitory on the third floor, requiring frequent use of stairs. He reports managing high levels of stress related to balancing his demanding academic schedule with his athletic commitments. He denies smoking and reports occasional social alcohol use.

imaging: None performed to date. The team's athletic trainer made a presumptive clinical diagnosis of Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome (PFPS) and recommended a formal physical therapy evaluation.
title: Case Study: Michael, a Collegiate Runner with Anterior Knee Pain

clinial_notes:
Clinical History

Mrs. Evelyn Wilson is a 63-year-old retired librarian who presents with a 5-year history of right knee pain, gradually worsening over the past year. She describes the pain as a deep ache with intermittent episodes of sharp catching sensations, particularly noticeable upon rising from a seated position and during ambulation. Stiffness is worst in the mornings and after prolonged periods of inactivity, while swelling develops after longer walks or household activities. She reports a reduction in her walking distance, increasing reliance on handrails when negotiating stairs, and difficulty kneeling or squatting. Mrs. Wilson reports disturbed sleep due to discomfort when changing positions at night. No history of recent trauma is noted, though she underwent an appendectomy at age 20 and has a longstanding diagnosis of hypertension.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - right medial knee joint - constant aching pain NPRS: 5-7

P2 - right lateral knee and lower thigh - intermittent catching/sharp pain NPRS: 3-4

aggrevating factors: Standing/walking longer than 30 minutes, climbing stairs (particularly descending), squatting, rising from chair, weather changes (damp/cold).

easing factors: Sitting with leg elevated, use of a heating pad, slow-paced walking on even surfaces, use of acetaminophen as needed.

past history No prior history of significant musculoskeletal trauma. Sedentary occupation for over three decades. Reports occasional low back pain, non-limiting.

medical history: Diagnosed hypertension managed by amlodipine for 10 years. No diabetes, no cardiac history. Appendectomy at age 20.

medications: Acetaminophen 500mg TID PRN for pain; Amlodipine 5mg daily for hypertension.

Clinical History

Michael Holland is a 42-year-old male, recreational distance runner, who presents with a 6-month history of progressively worsening pain in his right Achilles tendon. The discomfort began insidiously, initially noticeable only after morning runs, and has gradually increased in both frequency and intensity. Michael describes stiffness and pain at the posterior aspect of the ankle, particularly evident on rising in the morning and during the first few steps after periods of rest. Over the past month, he has also noted localized swelling and occasional crepitus in the tendon region. Despite modifying his running regime by reducing weekly mileage and switching to softer surfaces, he continues to experience persistent pain, which now sometimes limits his ability to train. He denies any history of recent trauma but recalls a mild ankle sprain on the same side two years ago. Recently, he has started over-the-counter NSAIDs with minimal relief.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - right midportion Achilles tendon (insertional and non-insertional portions) NPRS: 4-7

P2 - distal calf musculature (secondary discomfort with prolonged running) NPRS: 1-3

aggrevating factors: Running (especially uphill or speedwork), prolonged walking, climbing stairs, jumping, rising onto toes, and returning to activity after periods of rest.

easing factors: Resting, application of ice packs after activity, gentle stretching of the calf muscles, and wearing supportive footwear. Partial relief with NSAIDs.

past history Mild right ankle inversion sprain 2 years ago; full recovery reported at the time, no ongoing instability. No prior Achilles tendon issues.

medical history: Otherwise healthy. No history of systemic inflammatory disease, diabetes, or peripheral vascular issues. No known drug allergies. Non-smoker.

medications: Occasional ibuprofen (200-400mg prn), mainly post-run.

personal history: Michael is an accountant, working primarily at a desk. Runs 30-40 km per week as part of an amateur club. No history of elite sports participation. Recently increased training intensity in preparation for a half-marathon. Rare alcohol use. Married with two young children.

imaging: No imaging to date, though clinical examination shows thickening and tenderness of the right Achilles tendon 3 cm above the calcaneal insertion, with a mild palpable nodule. Mr. Robert Peterson is a 68-year-old retired general contractor who presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of chronic, progressive pain in both knees, with the right being significantly more troublesome than the left. He reports the onset has been insidious over the past 10-15 years but has worsened considerably in the last 2 years, now impacting his daily activities. He describes the pain (P1) in his right knee as a 'deep, gnawing ache' localized primarily around the medial (inner) aspect and just below the kneecap. He experiences intermittent sharp pain with certain movements, such as twisting or navigating stairs. He also notes a persistent 'background ache' in his left knee (P2), which is more generalized. A pronounced grinding or 'crunching' sound (crepitus) is noted in his right knee with nearly all movements. His primary goal is to walk his dog for more than 15 minutes and to be able to garden without suffering severe pain for the following two days.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - Right Knee - Medial joint line and peripatellar region (deep, gnawing ache with intermittent sharp pain) NPRS: 4-7/10

P2 - Left Knee - Generalized background ache NPRS: 2-4/10

aggrevating factors: Walking for more than 15-20 minutes, descending stairs (provokes sharp pain in P1), prolonged standing (e.g., while cooking), squatting or kneeling (making gardening nearly impossible), and rising from a seated position, particularly from a low chair. He also notes increased stiffness and aching during cold, damp weather.

easing factors: Short periods of rest, applying a heating pad to both knees, using a single-point cane (though he is reluctant to use it in public), and taking over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medication. Gentle cycling on a stationary bike for 10 minutes provides temporary relief from stiffness.

past history Mr. Peterson reports a right knee injury in his late 20s while playing recreational football, which he believes was a 'meniscus tear' but was never surgically addressed. He has a long history of physically demanding work as a contractor, involving frequent kneeling, heavy lifting, and climbing ladders. He has not had any prior physical therapy for his knees.

medical history: He is generally in good health but has been diagnosed with Hypertension, which is well-managed with medication. He has a Body Mass Index (BMI) of 31, placing him in the obese category.

medications: Lisinopril 10mg daily (for Hypertension), Ibuprofen 400mg as needed (typically takes it 3-4 times per week for knee pain).

personal history: Retired, lives with his wife in a two-story home. He finds the stairs to be a significant daily obstacle. He was previously very active, enjoying hiking, fishing, and extensive gardening. His current activity level is greatly diminished due to his knee pain, which he finds very frustrating and has negatively impacted his mood. He is motivated to engage in therapy to avoid or delay potential knee replacement surgery.

imaging: Weight-bearing X-rays of both knees performed 3 months prior. Report indicates moderate to severe tricompartmental osteoarthritis. Clinical History

Mrs. Patricia Liu, a 68-year-old retired librarian, presents with a 1-week history of sudden mid-thoracic back pain following bending over to retrieve a book from a low shelf at home. She describes the pain as sharp and localized over the mid-back, with no significant radiation. She notes increased pain during activities involving trunk flexion or prolonged standing, and reports difficulty sleeping due to pain when turning in bed. She does not recall any major trauma. NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - mid-thoracic spine (vertebral bodies T7-T9) NPRS: 6-8

P2 - paraspinal muscles adjacent to the area, soreness from muscle spasm NPRS: 2-4

aggrevating factors: Forward bending, rising from a chair, lifting objects, prolonged standing, coughing/sneezing.

easing factors: Resting with the back supported; reclining in a semi-upright position; heat application to paraspinal muscles; short walks indoors.

past history Diagnosed with early menopause at age 44; sustained a distal radius (wrist) fracture 5 years ago after a fall. No previous history of spinal fractures.

medical history: History of hypertension (well controlled) and hypothyroidism. No history of malignancy.

medications: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation; Bisphosphonate therapy (Alendronate, initiated 2 years ago); Levothyroxine; Lisinopril.

personal history: Lives alone, widowed; non-smoker, does not consume alcohol regularly; walks 15-20 minutes daily but limited during winter; diet reportedly low in dairy products for many years.

imaging: [Recent thoracic spine X-ray: compression fracture at T8 vertebral body with >25% loss of anterior vertebral height; evidence of osteopenia in adjacent vertebral bodies.]

clinial_notes:
Clinical History

Michael is a 20-year-old male collegiate soccer player (midfielder) who presents with acute onset of left posterior thigh pain. The injury occurred 2 days ago during a competitive match. He was accelerating into a full sprint to chase a loose ball when he felt a sudden, sharp 'popping' sensation in the back of his left thigh. The pain was immediate and severe, causing him to pull up and fall to the ground. He was unable to continue playing and was assisted off the field by the athletic trainer. He reports immediate difficulty with weight-bearing and a significant limp. Over the next 24 hours, he noted progressive swelling and the development of ecchymosis (bruising) extending down the back of his thigh towards the knee. His primary complaint (P1) is a sharp, localized pain in the mid-belly of his left hamstring, with a secondary ache (P2) in his left gluteal region from altered gait mechanics.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - Sharp, localized pain in the posterior mid-thigh (belly of the biceps femoris) NPRS: 6-8

P2 - Dull ache in the left gluteal region NPRS: 2-3

aggrevating factors: Walking for more than 5-10 minutes, ascending/descending stairs, attempting to jog or run, active knee flexion against resistance, passive knee extension (straightening the leg), forward bending (touching toes), prolonged sitting (especially in a low chair), and pressing the gas/clutch pedal while driving.

easing factors: Rest with the leg elevated, application of ice pack (20 minutes every 2 hours), gentle compression with a thigh sleeve, and using crutches to offload the leg.

past history History of a minor Grade I left hamstring strain approximately 18 months ago, during the previous season. He received brief treatment from the team's athletic trainer but admits he did not complete the full strengthening protocol as the season ended and the pain resolved with rest.

medical history: Generally fit and well. No other musculoskeletal injuries. No known allergies. All immunizations are up to date.

medications: Taking Ibuprofen 400mg, 3 times per day for the past 2 days.

personal history: Full-time student on a soccer scholarship, studying Kinesiology. Lives in a dormitory on campus. He is highly motivated to return to play as soon as possible due to an upcoming championship tournament. He denies smoking but reports occasional social alcohol use with teammates.

imaging: None to date. Clinical diagnosis is a Grade II hamstring strain. An MRI would be considered if there is suspicion of a full-thickness tear (Grade III) or avulsion fracture, or if progress stalls.

clinial_notes:
Clinical History

Mr. John Carter is a 48-year-old construction worker who underwent an above-knee (transfemoral) amputation of his right leg six months ago following a traumatic worksite accident involving a heavy machinery rollover. He reports residual limb pain and significant discomfort at the distal end of the stump, particularly after prolonged use of his prosthesis. He also complains of phantom limb sensations, describing intermittent sharp pain and tingling perceived in his absent foot. Mr. Carter presents for a physical therapy consultation with the primary goal of improving his mobility, optimizing prosthetic use, and managing his pain.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - Distal residual limb (right femur, soft tissue around amputation site) NPRS: 3-6

P2 - Phantom limb pain (perceived in absent right foot and calf) NPRS: 2-5

aggrevating factors: Extended prosthetic use (over 2-3 hours), walking on uneven surfaces, prolonged standing, cold weather, and at night during periods of inactivity.

easing factors: Removing prosthesis for rest, gentle stump massage, use of a heated pad, and over-the-counter acetaminophen. Engages in relaxation exercises for phantom pain.

past history No prior musculoskeletal injuries to the lower limbs. No significant medical comorbidities prior to the accident. Occasional back discomfort due to years of manual labor.

medical history: Otherwise healthy. No diabetes, vascular disease, or prior surgeries. No history of depression, though recent mood changes have been noted post-amputation.

medications: Acetaminophen 500 mg PRN for pain; Gabapentin 100 mg daily for phantom limb pain (recently prescribed); Topical antibiotic ointment applied to residual limb to reduce risk of infection.

personal history: Lives with his wife and two teenage children in a single-story home. Was the primary income earner prior to his accident. Enjoyed recreational cycling and hiking before injury. Mild to moderate difficulty adjusting psychologically to loss of limb and changes to body image; expresses interest in returning to adapted sports.

imaging: Postoperative X-ray confirmed appropriate femoral stump length and soft tissue coverage with no heterotopic ossification; recent ultrasound showed no evidence of residual limb infection or deep vein thrombosis.
title: Rehabilitation of a Transfemoral Amputee: The Case of Mr. John Carter

He reports sharp pain during the first steps after sitting for extended periods, going up stairs, and during the stance phase of running. Resting or reducing activity offers mild relief, but pain often returns when activity is resumed. James also notes episodes of night pain when turning in bed and occasional stiffness in the morning that resolves after about 15â€“20 minutes. P2 - deep anterior hip (iliopsoas region) NPRS: 2-3

aggrevating factors: Running (especially uphill or long distances), prolonged walking (>30 min), standing on one leg (single-leg balance), climbing stairs, transitioning from sitting to standing, crossing legs, lying on affected side.

easing factors: Rest, reduced activity, gentle stretching, ice after activity, side-lying on the unaffected side with a pillow between the knees.

clinial_notes:
Clinical History

Mr. Robert H., a 48-year-old warehouse worker, presents with a 6-month history of persistent low back pain. The pain began insidiously after several months of increased overtime shifts requiring frequent lifting and prolonged stooping. He describes a deep, aching discomfort centralized over the lumbar spine, occasionally radiating to the right buttock (but not below the knee). He rates his primary pain as moderate to severe, worse by the end of his workday. He reports associated morning stiffness lasting up to 30 minutes and periodic sleep disruption due to discomfort when rolling in bed. The pain intensity fluctuates with activity levels, and he notes that it tends to increase with prolonged standing, lifting heavy objects, or forward bending. Sitting with adequate back support or lying supine with knees bent provides some relief. He has no lower limb weakness, numbness, or changes in bowel/bladder function.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - central lower lumbar region (L4-L5, L5-S1 paraspinals and multifidus) NPRS: 5-7

P2 - intermittent right gluteal pain (gluteus maximus, piriformis) NPRS: 2-4

aggrevating factors: Prolonged standing (>30 minutes), repetitive lifting or bending, twisting movements, sitting on low chairs, driving for long durations, coughing or sneezing (mildly aggravating).

easing factors: Rest in supine with knees bent, supportive chair with lumbar roll, use of hot packs, over-the-counter NSAIDs, gentle walking.

past history Two minor episodes of acute low back pain in his late thirties, both resolving within a week. No trauma or prior surgeries. History of mild obesity and sedentary lifestyle outside of work.

medical history: Borderline hypertension controlled with diet, BMI 29. No diabetes or systemic illness.

medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg as needed (up to twice daily), occasional use of topical analgesic cream.

personal history: Married, two adolescent children. High job stress due to recent layoffs at work. Reports limited time for recreational activity; no structured exercise routine. Non-smoker, occasional alcohol. Feels increased job insecurity and worries about providing for his family.

imaging: Lumbar spine X-ray shows mild degenerative disc changes at L4-L5 and L5-S1, no evidence of fracture or malignancy. No red flag findings.
title: Chronic Low Back Pain in a Manual Laborer: The Case of Mr. Robert H.

Clinical History

Mr. George Lawson is an 81-year-old retired postal worker who lives independently. He was admitted to the emergency department following a mechanical fall at home. Mr. Lawson tripped over a rug in his hallway and landed directly on his left side. He immediately experienced severe left hip pain and was unable to bear weight. In the emergency room, physical examination revealed shortening and external rotation of the left lower limb. There was marked tenderness over the left hip and decreased range of motion due to pain. Radiographs confirmed a displaced intertrochanteric fracture of the left femur.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - left hip/groin â€“ primary fracture site NPRS: 8-9

P2 - left thigh â€“ referred muscular pain due to surrounding tissue trauma NPRS: 5-6

aggrevating factors: Attempted movement of the left lower limb (particularly abduction and rotation), weight-bearing, transfers from bed to chair, and any attempts at sitting up put significant stress on the involved area.

easing factors: Immobilization, positioning with pillows to support the limb, regular administration of opioids and acetaminophen, application of ice, and minimal movement. Slight relief with limb elevation.

past history History of hypertension and two minor falls in the past year but previously ambulant with a cane. No previous hip fractures.

medical history: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, well-controlled type 2 diabetes. No known osteoporosis diagnosis, but was never screened. No history of malignancy.

medications: Lisinopril 10mg daily, Atorvastatin 20mg nightly, Metformin 500mg twice daily, Acetaminophen 1g q6h prn, Morphine 5mg IV q4h prn post-injury.

personal history: Lives alone in a one-story apartment. Widowed 7 years ago. Two adult children visit weekly. Independent with activities of daily living prior to injury; enjoyed gardening and daily walks with a neighbor. Limited social activity beyond family.

imaging: AP and lateral X-ray of the pelvis and left femur showed a displaced intertrochanteric fracture of the left femur, no acetabular involvement.

Clinical History

Samuel Bennett is a 44-year-old male, IT consultant, and recreational long-distance runner who presents with a 7-month history of gradually increasing pain and stiffness localized to his right Achilles tendon. He reports the onset of symptoms soon after increasing his weekly mileage in preparation for an upcoming half marathon. Initially, he experienced morning stiffness in the posterior ankle area that eased after walking for a few minutes but would return and worsen after intense runs, hill intervals, or prolonged upright activity. Over recent weeks, the pain has become more persistent and begins earlier in his runs. Symptoms are now impacting his ability to complete training sessions, and he has noticed some mild swelling approximately 3 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion. He denies acute trauma or systemic symptoms but describes difficulty with activities such as descending stairs and pushing off during walking. No neurological symptoms. No night pain. Occasional use of ice and over-the-counter anti-inflammatories provides partial relief.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - mid-portion of right Achilles tendon NPRS: 5-7

P2 - posterior right heel (secondary, only after long activity) NPRS: 2-3

aggrevating factors: Running (especially on hills or speed work), prolonged walking or standing, descending stairs, wearing low-heeled or unsupportive shoes.

easing factors: Rest, icing, gentle stretching, use of cushioned footwear, reduced activity levels.

past history No previous history of Achilles or other significant lower limb injuries. History of mild plantar fasciitis two years prior, resolved with conservative management.

medical history: Unremarkable. No history of inflammatory or metabolic disease. No recent corticosteroid or fluoroquinolone use.

medications: Occasional ibuprofen (400 mg) as needed post-activity.

personal history: Works from home, high-stress but mainly sedentary job. Married with two school-aged children. Non-smoker, drinks alcohol socially, maintains a balanced diet. Increased running volume recently to support personal fitness goals during the COVID-19 pandemic.

imaging: No imaging conducted to date. Clinically diagnosed; consideration for musculoskeletal ultrasound if symptoms persist or worsen.

James, a 34-year-old construction worker, was playing a recreational basketball game last weekend. While attempting to defend an opposing player, he landed awkwardly on his right foot resulting in excessive inversion of the ankle. He immediately felt a sharp pain and was unable to continue playing, having to be helped to the sideline. The ankle began to swell significantly within an hour, and by the following morning, there was notable bruising around the lateral aspect of his ankle. James reports persistent pain when trying to bear weight, and he notices instability or a 'rolling' sensation when attempting to walk.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - lateral aspect of the right ankle NPRS: 6-8

aggrevating factors: weight-bearing activities, especially walking and going downstairs. His job involves standing and walking on uneven surfaces, which also increases pain.

easing factors: keeping the foot elevated, applying ice, and taking over-the-counter ibuprofen

past history James has had previous ankle sprains on the same side during his high school years but had no issues in recent years.

medical history: non-contributory

medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg every 8 hours for pain management

personal history: James lives an active lifestyle, regularly engaging in outdoor sports. Married with two children, he maintains a busy schedule balancing family and work.

imaging: X-ray conducted in the emergency room showed no fractures but evidence of soft tissue swelling.

clinial_notes:
Clinical History

Mrs. Linda Brown is a 47-year-old administrative assistant who presents with a 4-year history of generalized muscle pain and fatigue. Her primary complaints include persistent, diffuse aching and stiffness in the neck, shoulders, upper and lower back, and hips. The pain is present daily, fluctuates in intensity, and is often accompanied by sleep disturbances, unrefreshing sleep, intermittent headaches, and episodes of 'brain fog' affecting memory and concentration. She reports that the symptoms have slowly worsened over the last year, particularly after a period of heightened work-related stress. She denies significant joint swelling or redness. There is no associated fever, weight loss, or rashes.

NPRS is on a scale of 0-10

P1 - bilateral trapezius, rhomboids, lumbar paraspinals, and gluteal muscles NPRS: 5-7

P2 - quadriceps and forearm extensors NPRS: 3-5

aggrevating factors: Prolonged sitting or standing, cold or damp weather, elevated stress, poor-quality sleep, and excessive physical activity.

easing factors: Warm showers, gentle stretching, low-impact aerobic exercise (e.g., walking, swimming), cognitive behavioral relaxation techniques, and regular sleep routine.

past history No significant trauma or surgery. Occasional mild anxiety episodes in the past, otherwise healthy.

medical history: No history of inflammatory arthritis, autoimmune disorders, or neuropathies. Diagnosed with mild depression 2 years ago, managed non-pharmacologically.

medications: Duloxetine 30 mg daily for pain and mood stabilization, paracetamol as needed, magnesium supplement, and occasional use of melatonin for sleep.

personal history: Lives with spouse, has two teenage children. Sedentary work. Former amateur tennis player until symptoms worsened. Reports high work pressure and feels responsible for elderly parent care, adding to her stress load.

imaging: Previous cervical and lumbar spine X-rays and MRI unremarkable; no evidence of structural pathology.
title: Complex Widespread Pain in a Middle-Aged Female with Fibromyalgia
